_meta.note: Science cases and anecdotes in Weekly's own words. Caveats state myths, failed replications and ethics honestly.

gage.title: Phineas Gage and the tamping iron
gage.who_when: Phineas Gage, railroad construction foreman; physician John Martyn Harlow; Cavendish, Vermont, 1848
gage.story: Gage was packing blasting powder into a rock with a long iron rod when a spark set it off. The rod, more than a meter long, shot up through his left cheek, behind his eye and out the top of his skull, landing many meters away. Astonishingly, he sat up, talked, and survived. His doctor, John Harlow, later wrote that the careful, well-liked foreman had become impatient, profane and unable to stick to his plans, so much that friends said he was no longer the same man.
gage.shows: The front of the brain helps hold plans, manners and impulse control together; damage there can change character while leaving speech, strength and memory intact.
gage.caveat: The story grew in the retelling. Historian Malcolm Macmillan's research suggests Gage later recovered a good deal: he worked for years driving a stagecoach in Chile, a job that demanded planning and self-control. That recovery is itself a lesson: the brain can relearn with structure and routine.
gage.source: John M. Harlow's case reports (1848, 1868); Malcolm Macmillan, An Odd Kind of Fame (2000)

elliot.title: Elliot, the man who could not decide
elliot.who_when: Patient 'Elliot', studied by neurologist Antonio Damasio, USA, 1980s
elliot.story: Elliot had been a capable businessman and family man until surgery removed a brain tumor along with tissue in the lower front of his brain. Afterwards his IQ, memory and reasoning tests looked normal, yet his life fell apart: lost jobs, a failed marriage, ruinous investments. Damasio describes him spending ages weighing trivial choices, such as how to sort papers, and calmly describing tragedies, including his own, without feeling a thing. Shown disturbing pictures, he said he knew he should be upset but was not.
elliot.shows: Feelings are not the enemy of good choices; they tag options as good or bad and make deciding possible. Damasio called these signals somatic markers.
elliot.caveat: A single patient, described years later in a popular book; the somatic marker hypothesis remains influential but debated, and other researchers explain these patients' problems in different ways.

hm.title: H.M., the man who lived in the present
hm.who_when: Henry Molaison ('H.M.'), surgeon William Scoville, psychologist Brenda Milner; Hartford, Connecticut, 1953 onward
hm.story: To stop severe seizures, a surgeon removed parts of Henry Molaison's brain on both sides, including the hippocampus. The seizures eased, but Henry could no longer form new lasting memories: he could chat warmly with a researcher and not know her when she returned after a break. Yet when Brenda Milner had him trace a star while watching only its mirror image, he got better day after day, while insisting each time he had never tried it before.
hm.shows: Memory is not one thing. Knowing facts and events depends on different brain systems from learning skills and habits, which can grow without any conscious memory of practicing.
hm.caveat: The surgery was experimental and would never be done today. Henry was studied by many researchers for over fifty years and could not meaningfully consent to all of it, which raises lasting ethical questions.
hm.source: Scoville & Milner (1957); Suzanne Corkin, Permanent Present Tense (2013)

clive-wearing.title: Clive Wearing's thirty-second world
clive-wearing.who_when: Clive Wearing, British musician; wife Deborah Wearing; England, from 1985
clive-wearing.story: A viral brain infection destroyed much of Clive Wearing's memory. Since then he has lived in a window of seconds, constantly feeling he has just woken for the first time; his diaries are filled with lines announcing that he is now truly awake, each earlier line crossed out. Yet he can still sit at a piano and play or conduct with skill, and whenever his wife Deborah walks in he greets her with overwhelming joy, as if after a long absence.
clive-wearing.shows: Identity and love can survive the loss of memory, and practiced skills live in a different system from remembered events.
clive-wearing.caveat: Retellings sometimes say he forgets everything instantly; in reality some feelings, habits and familiar routines persist, which is part of what makes his case so moving.

patient-sm.title: Patient S.M., the woman without fear
patient-sm.who_when: Patient 'S.M.', studied by Justin Feinstein, Ralph Adolphs, Daniel Tranel and colleagues, University of Iowa, reported 2011
patient-sm.story: A rare genetic condition destroyed both of S.M.'s amygdalae, small almond-shaped structures deep in the brain. Researchers took her to a pet shop, where she reached for snakes and spiders staff told her to avoid, and to a haunted house, where she poked a costumed monster. Her life history shows she was held up at knifepoint and threatened with death, yet reported feeling no fear, and she kept walking into the same risky places.
patient-sm.shows: Fear is a protective signal that keeps us away from danger; without it, people repeat risky situations because nothing inside says stop.
patient-sm.caveat: One person, so caution with broad claims. Later work found she could feel intense panic when asked to inhale carbon dioxide, showing that fear arising from inside the body uses other routes.
patient-sm.source: Feinstein et al. (2011, Current Biology); Feinstein et al. (2013, Nature Neuroscience)

korsakoff.title: Korsakoff's patients and the filled-in past
korsakoff.who_when: Sergei Korsakoff, Russian psychiatrist, 1880s; later research on thiamine deficiency
korsakoff.story: Korsakoff described long-term heavy drinkers who could not hold on to new information, yet calmly told invented stories to fill the gaps, describing a walk they never took or a visitor who never came. They were not lying on purpose. We now know the syndrome stems largely from a severe shortage of thiamine (vitamin B1), common in heavy drinking with poor diet, which damages memory circuits.
korsakoff.shows: Alcohol harms the brain both directly and through malnutrition, and the brain will fill empty memories with confident fiction.
korsakoff.caveat: Not every heavy drinker develops it, and early treatment with thiamine can prevent or limit the damage, which is why it matters medically.

brain-recovery.title: Brains that heal in abstinence
brain-recovery.who_when: Nora Volkow and colleagues, Brookhaven National Laboratory, reported 2001
brain-recovery.story: Brain scans of people who had used methamphetamine heavily showed fewer dopamine transporters, the machinery that recycles dopamine. When the researchers scanned some of the same people again after more than a year without the drug, those markers had recovered substantially. Their memory and movement tests, though, had not bounced back as fully, a sign that healing is real but slow and uneven.
brain-recovery.shows: Some drug-related brain changes partly reverse with sustained abstinence; time without use is itself a treatment.
brain-recovery.caveat: Small samples, and recovery differs by drug, amount and person. The images do not show that damage is fully undone, nor exactly how changes relate to everyday behavior.
brain-recovery.source: Volkow et al. (2001, Journal of Neuroscience)

rat-park.title: Rat Park: cages, colonies and morphine
rat-park.who_when: Bruce Alexander and colleagues, Simon Fraser University, Canada, late 1970s
rat-park.story: Classic addiction studies kept rats alone in small cages with drug-laced water, and the rats took a lot. Alexander suspected the cage itself. His team built Rat Park, a roomy enclosure with toys, wheels, food and many other rats to mingle and mate with. Offered the same choice between plain water and morphine water, the Rat Park rats generally took far less of the drug than isolated rats.
rat-park.shows: Environment, isolation and lack of alternatives shape drug-taking, not only the drug's chemistry.
rat-park.caveat: The studies were small and published in a modest journal; attempts to repeat them gave mixed results. Wider research on enriched environments supports the general point, but the popular claim that addiction is simply about cages oversimplifies it.
rat-park.source: Alexander, Coambs & Hadaway (1978); Alexander et al. (1981)

vietnam-heroin.title: Vietnam veterans who left heroin behind
vietnam-heroin.who_when: Lee Robins and colleagues, Washington University in St. Louis; US soldiers returning from Vietnam, early 1970s
vietnam-heroin.story: Cheap, strong heroin was easy to get in Vietnam, and many American soldiers became dependent on it there. Officials feared an epidemic when they came home. Sociologist Lee Robins followed the returning men and found that only a small minority of those who had been addicted in Vietnam became readdicted once they were back in the United States, many without any treatment.
vietnam-heroin.shows: Leaving the setting where use happened, with its cues, stress and availability, can sharply change the course of addiction; recovery without formal treatment is more common than people assume.
vietnam-heroin.caveat: These were mostly young men whose use began in a war zone; those who did relapse often had problems before the war. It does not mean addiction is easy to quit, especially when people return to the same neighborhood and people.

olds-milner.title: The rat that would not stop pressing
olds-milner.who_when: James Olds and Peter Milner, McGill University, Montreal, 1954
olds-milner.story: Olds and Milner placed a thin electrode in a rat's brain, slightly off target as it turned out. The rat kept returning to the corner of its box where it had been stimulated. When the researchers let rats press a lever to stimulate that area themselves, some pressed it thousands of times an hour, ignoring food and pushing on until they collapsed.
olds-milner.shows: The brain has reward circuits that can hijack behavior, and drugs act on these same systems more directly than ordinary pleasures.
olds-milner.caveat: It was hailed as the pleasure center, but later research suggests these circuits drive wanting and seeking more than pleasure itself. Similar stimulation experiments on humans in the 1950s and 60s are now seen as ethically troubling.

wanting-liking.title: Wanting without liking
wanting-liking.who_when: Kent Berridge and Terry Robinson, University of Michigan, 1990s onward
wanting-liking.story: Berridge's team studied rats whose dopamine had been largely depleted. The rats stopped seeking food and would starve without help. Yet when sugar water was placed in their mouths, they still made the same lip-licking 'yum' faces as normal rats. Dopamine, it seemed, was not needed for liking sweetness, only for wanting and pursuing it. Rats repeatedly given drugs such as amphetamine became hypersensitive to reward cues and worked harder for them, while their liking reactions to the reward itself did not grow.
wanting-liking.shows: Addiction can grow a powerful wanting system that keeps craving long after the drug stops feeling good: the incentive-sensitization theory.
wanting-liking.caveat: Most evidence comes from animals; in people, wanting and liking overlap and are harder to measure. It is a leading theory, not the whole story.

siegel-tolerance.title: Siegel's rats: overdose in an unfamiliar room
siegel-tolerance.who_when: Shepard Siegel and colleagues, McMaster University, Canada, 1982
siegel-tolerance.story: Rats were given rising doses of heroin, always in the same setting, until they tolerated amounts that would kill a newcomer. Then each got a large dose. Rats dosed in their usual room mostly survived; rats dosed in a strange room died at a much higher rate. The body had learned to brace for the drug when it saw familiar cues, and without those cues the brace was missing.
siegel-tolerance.shows: Tolerance is partly learned: the body links surroundings and rituals with the drug, which helps explain some human overdoses in unusual places and why cues trigger withdrawal-like craving.
siegel-tolerance.caveat: Animal work. Human overdoses have many causes, including mixing drugs and unpredictable potency such as fentanyl; context is one factor among several.

release-overdose.title: The deadly weeks after release
release-overdose.who_when: Ingrid Binswanger and colleagues, study of people released from Washington State prisons, published 2007
release-overdose.story: Researchers linked prison release records with death records and found that in the first two weeks after leaving prison, former prisoners died at a rate many times higher than other residents, with drug overdose the leading cause. Later studies in other countries found the same pattern. Tolerance falls during incarceration, but old habits, places and doses wait outside. Researchers point to lost tolerance: a dose the body handled before prison can stop breathing after it.
release-overdose.shows: Lowered tolerance plus return to familiar cues makes the first days home a period of extreme overdose risk; planning, naloxone and treatment continuity save lives.
release-overdose.caveat: Figures vary by place and period, and the rise of fentanyl has changed the risk since. The pattern of high early danger has held up across many studies.
release-overdose.source: Binswanger et al. (2007, New England Journal of Medicine)

balanced-placebo.title: The tonic that made people drink
balanced-placebo.who_when: G. Alan Marlatt, Barbara Demming and John Reid, University of Washington, 1973
balanced-placebo.story: Heavy drinkers and social drinkers were asked to rate the taste of drinks. Some were told they had vodka and tonic, some plain tonic, and in each group half really got alcohol while the rest did not. How much people went on to drink depended on what they believed was in the glass, not on what actually was. Believing they had alcohol led to more drinking even when they had none.
balanced-placebo.shows: Expectations about a drug's effects drive behavior powerfully, so the idea that one drink triggers uncontrollable loss of control is largely a belief, not chemistry.
balanced-placebo.caveat: The design works only with low doses that people cannot taste or feel; it cannot show that expectations matter as much at heavy intoxication.
balanced-placebo.source: Marlatt, Demming & Reid (1973, Journal of Abnormal Psychology)

marlatt-relapse.title: Marlatt's map of how relapse happens
marlatt-relapse.who_when: G. Alan Marlatt and colleagues, late 1970s-1980s, USA
marlatt-relapse.story: Instead of assuming relapse was random weakness, Marlatt asked people who had returned to drinking, smoking, heroin or gambling to describe exactly when and where it happened. Across very different substances the same situations kept appearing: negative emotions such as anger, boredom or depression, conflict with another person, and social pressure. Relapse usually followed a chain of small decisions that looked harmless at the time.
marlatt-relapse.shows: Relapse is predictable and preventable: it follows identifiable high-risk situations and chains of 'apparently irrelevant decisions' that can be spotted and interrupted.
marlatt-relapse.caveat: Later research found relapse more complex and dynamic than a fixed list of triggers; the categories are a helpful map, not a full explanation.

project-match.title: Project MATCH: three roads, similar results
project-match.who_when: US National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, multisite trial, 1990s
project-match.story: Researchers had a hopeful idea: match each drinker to the treatment that suits him or her. Over a thousand people were randomly assigned to cognitive-behavioral therapy, motivational enhancement therapy or Twelve Step facilitation. Most clients in all three improved substantially, and the predicted perfect matches mostly did not appear. One hint did: very angry clients did comparatively well in the brief motivational approach.
project-match.shows: Several well-delivered approaches work, and the relationship, engagement and the client's own commitment may matter more than the label on the program.
project-match.caveat: There was no untreated group, so part of the improvement may reflect being in a careful study. Matching ideas were not proven wrong for every kind of client.
project-match.source: Project MATCH Research Group (1997, Journal of Studies on Alcohol)

higgins-vouchers.title: Paying people to stay clean
higgins-vouchers.who_when: Stephen Higgins and colleagues, University of Vermont, early 1990s
higgins-vouchers.story: Cocaine users in treatment earned vouchers each time their urine test came back clean, exchangeable for things like movie passes or sports gear. The value rose with each consecutive clean test and dropped back if they used. Compared with standard counseling, more people stayed in treatment and stayed abstinent longer. The approach, contingency management, is now one of the best-supported treatments for stimulant use.
higgins-vouchers.shows: Behavior responds to immediate, certain rewards; giving recovery its own quick payoff competes directly with the quick payoff of the drug.
higgins-vouchers.caveat: Effects often fade after the rewards stop, and some people object to paying for abstinence, even though the money is small next to the costs of addiction.
higgins-vouchers.source: Higgins et al. (1991, 1993, American Journal of Psychiatry)

dole-nyswander.title: Methadone and the right to work
dole-nyswander.who_when: Vincent Dole and Marie Nyswander, Rockefeller University, New York, mid-1960s
dole-nyswander.story: Dole, a metabolism researcher, and Nyswander, a psychiatrist who had worked with heroin users, gave a small group of long-term heroin users steady daily doses of methadone. Instead of spending their days hustling for the next fix, the patients stabilized: many returned to school or work and stopped committing crimes. Dole argued that heroin addiction behaved like a metabolic disease needing ongoing medicine.
dole-nyswander.shows: Medication can remove the craving and withdrawal cycle so that people can rebuild their lives, the starting point of medication-assisted treatment.
dole-nyswander.caveat: Methadone has risks, including overdose when misused, and its long history of stigma persists, including in some recovery groups. Medication works best with support, not alone.

cochrane-aa.title: AA under the microscope
cochrane-aa.who_when: John F. Kelly, Keith Humphreys and Marica Ferri, Cochrane review, 2020
cochrane-aa.story: For decades scientists argued whether Alcoholics Anonymous really works or simply attracts people already motivated to stop. A rigorous review pooled studies that compared AA and Twelve Step facilitation with other treatments such as CBT. It concluded that, for helping people stay abstinent, clinically delivered Twelve Step facilitation did as well as or better than the established therapies, and it tended to lower healthcare costs.
cochrane-aa.shows: Mutual-help groups can provide free, ongoing support that formal treatment cannot; linking people to them is a real intervention.
cochrane-aa.caveat: Most studies involved Twelve Step facilitation delivered by professionals rather than AA alone, and benefits depend on actual involvement. AA does not suit everyone; secular alternatives exist.
cochrane-aa.source: Kelly, Humphreys & Ferri (2020), Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews

bill-w.title: Two drunks in Akron
bill-w.who_when: Bill Wilson and Dr. Robert Smith, Akron, Ohio, 1935
bill-w.story: Bill Wilson, a New York stockbroker who had recently stopped drinking, was alone in Akron after a failed business deal and felt the pull of the hotel bar. He realized that talking to another alcoholic might keep him sober, phoned around, and was introduced to Bob Smith, a surgeon still drinking. Their long conversation, one drunk to another, became the seed of Alcoholics Anonymous.
bill-w.shows: Helping someone else with the same problem can protect the helper; mutual identification is a core change ingredient in self-help groups.
bill-w.caveat: The founding story is retold with a halo. Early AA made success claims that were never measured, and Wilson himself struggled with depression for years.

jung-letter.title: Jung's letter: spirit against spirits
jung-letter.who_when: Carl Jung and Bill Wilson, correspondence 1961; earlier, Jung's patient Rowland Hazard
jung-letter.story: Years before AA existed, an American businessman, Rowland Hazard, went to Carl Jung for help with drinking. Jung eventually told him his case was nearly hopeless unless he had a profound spiritual or religious experience. Hazard sought one, got sober, and passed the idea along, and it reached Bill Wilson. Decades later Wilson wrote to thank Jung, who replied that craving for alcohol could be a thirst for wholeness, summed up in a Latin phrase meaning spirit against spirits.
jung-letter.shows: Many recovery traditions see addiction as partly a search for meaning and connection that a substance answers falsely.
jung-letter.caveat: This is history and personal testimony, not experimental evidence; spirituality helps many people but is not required for recovery.
jung-letter.source: Letters between C. G. Jung and Bill W., 1961

doll-hill.title: The doctors who proved cigarettes kill
doll-hill.who_when: Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill, Britain, 1950 onward
doll-hill.story: In 1950, few doctors suspected smoking. Doll and Hill interviewed lung cancer patients in London hospitals and found they were far more likely to be heavy smokers than other patients. Doll gave up smoking because of his own data. They then followed tens of thousands of British doctors for decades; the smokers died of lung cancer, heart disease and other causes far sooner than non-smokers, and those who quit, even in middle age, regained much of the lost time.
doll-hill.shows: Tobacco is one of the deadliest substances people use, and quitting at any age pays off.
doll-hill.caveat: Early on, critics including tobacco-funded scientists argued the link was not causal; the evidence later became overwhelming.
doll-hill.source: Doll & Hill (1950, BMJ); British Doctors Study

fas.title: Naming fetal alcohol syndrome
fas.who_when: Kenneth Lyons Jones and David Smith, University of Washington, Seattle, 1973 (with earlier work in France by Paul Lemoine)
fas.story: Two physicians noticed a pattern among babies born to mothers who drank heavily during pregnancy: small size, particular facial features and later problems with learning and behavior. They gave it a name, fetal alcohol syndrome. Before then, many doctors assumed the womb shielded the baby from what the mother drank. Their report, building on earlier work by a French doctor, changed medical advice to pregnant women around the world within a few years.
fas.shows: Alcohol crosses into the developing child and can cause lifelong harm; the effects of drinking reach well beyond the drinker.
fas.caveat: Effects range widely, and many affected children are never diagnosed; no amount of drinking in pregnancy is known to be safe, but most guidance is precautionary.

goodwin-adoption.title: Danish adoptees and the family tree
goodwin-adoption.who_when: Donald Goodwin and colleagues, studies of Danish adoptees, 1973
goodwin-adoption.story: To separate genes from upbringing, researchers studied sons of alcoholic fathers who had been adopted as babies and raised by other families. These sons developed alcoholism at a clearly higher rate than adopted sons whose birth parents had no such history, even though they never grew up around their biological father's drinking. Twin studies later pointed the same way: identical twins are more alike in drinking problems than fraternal twins.
goodwin-adoption.shows: Vulnerability to alcohol problems runs partly in genes, which helps explain why some people get hooked faster and why family history is a real risk factor.
goodwin-adoption.caveat: Genes raise risk; they do not decide fate. Most children of people with alcoholism do not develop it, and environment, culture and choices still matter.
goodwin-adoption.source: Goodwin et al. (1973, Archives of General Psychiatry)

porter-jick.title: The one-paragraph letter that fed an epidemic
porter-jick.who_when: Jane Porter and Hershel Jick, letter in the New England Journal of Medicine, 1980
porter-jick.story: Porter and Jick wrote a short letter noting that among hospital patients given narcotics in their database, very few were recorded as becoming addicted. It was not a study of long-term pain treatment at home. Years later, marketers and doctors cited it hundreds of times as proof that opioids rarely cause addiction, helping justify widespread prescribing. The journal eventually added an editor's note warning readers about how it had been misused.
porter-jick.shows: Opioids prescribed for pain can lead to dependence, and a weak piece of evidence repeated often enough can feel like settled fact.
porter-jick.caveat: The authors did not claim what was later attributed to them; the misuse lay in the citing, not mainly in the letter.

levine-placebo.title: The placebo that naloxone could undo
levine-placebo.who_when: Jon Levine, Newton Gordon and Howard Fields, University of California, San Francisco, 1978
levine-placebo.story: Patients who had just had wisdom teeth removed were given a placebo, which many said eased their pain. When some were then given naloxone, the drug that blocks opioids, the placebo's pain relief faded. The belief that they had been treated had apparently triggered the brain's own opioids. It was among the first pieces of evidence that placebo pain relief has a measurable chemical basis rather than being imagined.
levine-placebo.shows: The brain makes its own painkillers, and expectation, attention and calm can partly switch them on, part of why non-drug pain tools are not 'just in your head'.
levine-placebo.caveat: Placebo effects are real but limited; they do not cure underlying disease, and how strong they are varies widely.

pavlov.title: Pavlov's dogs and the footsteps
pavlov.who_when: Ivan Pavlov, St. Petersburg, Russia, around 1900
pavlov.story: Pavlov won a Nobel Prize for studying digestion, measuring how much dogs salivated when fed. Then a nuisance appeared: the dogs began drooling before any food arrived, at the sight of the assistant who usually fed them or the sound of approaching footsteps. Pavlov turned the nuisance into a science, pairing neutral sounds such as a metronome or buzzer with food until the sound alone made the dogs salivate.
pavlov.shows: The body learns to react to signals that predict a reward; this is the root of cue-triggered craving, where a place, person or sound sets off a physical urge.
pavlov.caveat: The famous bell is partly legend; Pavlov used several kinds of signals. Conditioned responses also fade if the cue keeps appearing without the reward, the basis of extinction.

little-albert.title: Little Albert and the white rat
little-albert.who_when: John B. Watson and Rosalie Rayner, Johns Hopkins University, 1920
little-albert.story: A calm baby known as Albert happily reached for a white rat. Then, each time he touched it, the researchers struck a steel bar loudly behind his head. After several pairings, Albert cried and crawled away at the sight of the rat alone, and his fear spread to a rabbit, a dog, a fur coat and even a bearded mask.
little-albert.shows: Fears and strong emotional reactions can be learned through association and then spread to similar things, which helps explain why triggers multiply.
little-albert.caveat: Ethically unacceptable today, and Albert was never deconditioned. Scholars still dispute who he was and how healthy he was; the experiment had one child and loose methods, so its findings were overstated in textbooks.
little-albert.source: Watson & Rayner (1920, Journal of Experimental Psychology)

peter-rabbit.title: Peter and the rabbit: unlearning a fear
peter-rabbit.story: Peter, a toddler, was terrified of rabbits. Jones fed him a snack he loved while a caged rabbit sat at the far side of the room. Day by day, as long as Peter stayed calm, the rabbit came a little closer, until Peter let it nibble his fingers and played with it happily. Seeing other children relaxed with the rabbit helped too.
peter-rabbit.shows: What is learned by association can be unlearned step by step by pairing the feared thing with safety and something pleasant; this work is often called the beginning of behavior therapy.
peter-rabbit.caveat: One child, an early report; the principle has since been confirmed in exposure therapies, though modern methods are more structured.

bobo-doll.title: Bandura's Bobo doll
bobo-doll.who_when: Albert Bandura, Dorothea Ross and Sheila Ross, Stanford University, 1961
bobo-doll.story: Preschoolers watched an adult in a playroom attack an inflatable clown doll, hitting it with a mallet, kicking it and shouting phrases. Others saw an adult play quietly. Left alone with the doll later, children who had watched the aggressive adult copied the attack, often using the same words and moves. Later versions showed children were less likely to copy when the adult was punished.
bobo-doll.shows: People learn behavior by watching others, especially role models, without ever being rewarded themselves: observational learning, central to social learning theory.
bobo-doll.caveat: A doll built to be knocked down invites hitting; play aggression in a lab is not the same as real violence. Still, the core finding that we learn by observing is solid.

learned-helplessness.title: Learned helplessness, and the twist fifty years later
learned-helplessness.who_when: Martin Seligman, Steven Maier and colleagues, University of Pennsylvania, 1960s; revisited 2016
learned-helplessness.story: Dogs that had earlier received shocks they could not escape were later placed in a box where simply stepping over a low barrier ended the shock. Many lay down and endured it, while dogs without that history quickly learned to escape. The finding became a model of depression: experience teaches that nothing you do matters. Fifty years later Maier and Seligman, using brain research, revised it: passivity seems to be the default response to prolonged threat, and what is actually learned is that you have control.
learned-helplessness.shows: Repeated experiences of powerlessness can shut down effort; experiences of control and small wins are what build the brain's sense of 'I can do something'.
learned-helplessness.caveat: The original work caused real suffering to animals and would face strong objection today. The model captures part of depression, not all of it.

variable-reward.title: The slot machine schedule
variable-reward.who_when: B. F. Skinner and Charles Ferster, schedules of reinforcement, 1950s
variable-reward.story: Skinner and Ferster found that animals rewarded unpredictably, after a varying number of lever presses, worked hardest and kept going longest after rewards stopped. Animals rewarded every time quit soon after the reward dried up. Slot machines, scratch cards and the occasional great high run on the same unpredictable pattern. Even after rewards stop completely, a creature trained this way keeps pressing, because the next press has always possibly been the winning one.
variable-reward.shows: Unpredictable rewards produce the most persistent behavior, one reason gambling and drug-seeking are so hard to extinguish and why 'maybe this time' is so powerful.
variable-reward.caveat: Human behavior also depends on thinking, values and social context, so schedules explain persistence well but not every choice.

milgram.title: Milgram's shock machine
milgram.story: Ordinary men answered a newspaper ad for a memory study. As 'teacher', each was told to shock a 'learner' in the next room for every wrong answer, with the voltage rising each time. The learner, an actor, cried out, banged on the wall, then fell silent. When volunteers hesitated, a calm man in a gray coat said the experiment required them to continue. In the best-known version, about two thirds went all the way to the top switch.
milgram.shows: Ordinary people will do things they believe are wrong when an authority takes responsibility and the steps are small, a warning about 'just following orders' and small step-by-step slides.
milgram.caveat: Archival research by Gina Perry found the experimenter sometimes went off script and many participants doubted the shocks were real. Obedience varied hugely across versions, and many people did refuse, especially when someone else defied first.
milgram.source: Stanley Milgram, Obedience to Authority (1974); Gina Perry, Behind the Shock Machine (2012)

asch.title: Asch's lines: standing alone
asch.story: A student sat at a table with several others to judge which of three lines matched a sample line. The answer was obvious. But the others, all secretly working with the researcher, gave the same wrong answer on certain rounds. Many real participants went along with the group at least once, visibly uncomfortable. When just one other person gave the right answer, conformity dropped sharply.
asch.shows: Group pressure can bend judgment even when the truth is plain, and a single ally makes it much easier to say no.
asch.caveat: Textbooks often stress the conformity, but most answers were actually independent and many people never gave in. The study used college men in 1950s America; levels vary by culture and era.

prophecy-fails.title: When Prophecy Fails
prophecy-fails.who_when: Leon Festinger, Henry Riecken and Stanley Schachter, Chicago area, 1954
prophecy-fails.story: A woman told her followers that a flood would destroy the world on a certain December day, but that a flying saucer would rescue believers. Some quit jobs and gave away belongings. Festinger's team joined the group undercover. When midnight passed with no saucer and no flood, many did not give up. A new message announced the world had been spared thanks to their faith, and they began seeking publicity and converts more eagerly than before.
prophecy-fails.shows: When people have invested heavily in a belief, contradicting evidence can make them cling harder; reducing the discomfort of being wrong, cognitive dissonance, can trump facts.
prophecy-fails.caveat: A small group, and the undercover researchers may have influenced it. Not all members reacted the same way; some drifted away.
prophecy-fails.source: Festinger, Riecken & Schachter, When Prophecy Fails (1956)

stanford-prison.title: The Stanford Prison Experiment, reconsidered
stanford-prison.who_when: Philip Zimbardo and colleagues, Stanford University, August 1971
stanford-prison.story: College men were randomly assigned to be guards or prisoners in a mock prison in a university basement. Within days some guards became cruel, forcing humiliating routines, while prisoners rebelled, then broke down. The study, planned for two weeks, was stopped after six days, after graduate student Christina Maslach objected to what she saw. It became the most famous demonstration of how roles and situations can turn ordinary people harsh.
stanford-prison.shows: Settings and roles exert strong pressure on behavior, which matters for anyone who lives or works in a prison.
stanford-prison.caveat: Strong critiques: recordings and archives show guards were encouraged to be tough, some participants say they were acting, and there was no control group. A 2002 BBC prison study by Reicher and Haslam found very different dynamics. It is better seen as a demonstration than as proof.
stanford-prison.source: Thibault Le Texier (2019, American Psychologist); Reicher & Haslam (2006)

good-samaritan.title: The Good Samaritan in a hurry
good-samaritan.who_when: John Darley and Daniel Batson, Princeton Theological Seminary, 1973
good-samaritan.story: Seminary students were asked to give a short talk in another building; for some, the topic was the parable of the Good Samaritan. On the way each passed a man slumped in a doorway, coughing and groaning. Whether they stopped had little to do with their religiosity or their topic. What mattered most was whether they had been told they were late. Some hurrying students literally stepped over him.
good-samaritan.shows: Situations, especially time pressure, can override values; good intentions need slowing down and noticing to become good actions.
good-samaritan.caveat: A small sample of one kind of person in one setting, and the hurried students may have felt torn between helping the stranger and the researcher waiting for them.

genovese.title: Kitty Genovese and the 38 witnesses myth
genovese.who_when: Kitty Genovese, Kew Gardens, Queens, New York, March 1964
genovese.story: Kitty Genovese was murdered outside her apartment building. Two weeks later, a New York Times story claimed 38 neighbors watched the attack and did nothing. The story shocked the nation and inspired research on bystander apathy. Later investigations found far fewer people actually saw the attack, some thought it was a quarrel, at least one called the police, and a neighbor, Sophia Farrar, ran out and held Kitty as she died.
genovese.shows: Famous stories about human nature can be badly distorted, and the real version shows ordinary courage as well as confusion.
genovese.caveat: The bystander effect itself has lab support, yet a 2020 analysis of real CCTV footage of public conflicts in several countries found that at least one bystander stepped in during most incidents. The case that launched the idea was largely myth.

loftus-crash.title: Smashed versus hit: rewriting a memory
loftus-crash.who_when: Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer, University of Washington, 1974
loftus-crash.story: People watched films of car crashes, then estimated the speed. Those asked how fast the cars were going when they 'smashed' into each other gave higher estimates than those asked about cars that 'hit'. A week later, the 'smashed' group were more likely to remember broken glass, though none appeared in the film. Loftus later showed people could be led to recall childhood events that never happened.
loftus-crash.shows: Memory is reconstructed each time it is recalled, and wording shapes it; describing a problem with only the facts protects it from drift.
loftus-crash.caveat: Lab memories of films differ from emotional events, and the work sparked heated debates in courts and therapy. Memory is not useless, just changeable.

hostile-attribution.title: Hostile attribution bias
hostile-attribution.who_when: Kenneth Dodge and colleagues, from the 1980s
hostile-attribution.story: Boys watched or heard about ambiguous incidents: another child bumps your tower of blocks or spills milk on you, and it is unclear whether on purpose. Aggressive boys were much more likely to assume the other child meant it and to plan revenge. Dodge and colleagues found the pattern in many countries and ages, and that it predicts later aggression.
hostile-attribution.shows: How we read another person's intentions in an unclear moment shapes whether we fight; checking the assumption is a learnable skill.
hostile-attribution.caveat: The bias is partly learned from real hostile environments, where expecting threat can be protective; it is not simply a fault in the person.

robbers-cave.title: Robbers Cave: enemies by design
robbers-cave.who_when: Muzafer Sherif and colleagues, summer camp in Robbers Cave State Park, Oklahoma, 1954
robbers-cave.story: Two groups of eleven-year-old boys arrived at camp separately, named themselves the Eagles and the Rattlers, and were then put into competitions for prizes. Insults, raids and flag burning followed. Simply bringing them together for meals made things worse. What reduced the hostility were problems neither group could solve alone, like a broken water supply and a stalled truck that everyone had to pull.
robbers-cave.shows: Competition breeds hostility between groups, and shared goals that require cooperation can soften it.
robbers-cave.caveat: Gina Perry's archival research shows the researchers worked to provoke conflict, and an earlier attempt in 1953 failed when the boys refused to turn on each other. The study is better read as a story than a clean experiment.
robbers-cave.source: Muzafer Sherif et al. (1961); Gina Perry, The Lost Boys (2018)

criminal-personality.title: Yochelson and Samenow's thinking errors
criminal-personality.who_when: Samuel Yochelson and Stanton Samenow, St. Elizabeths Hospital, Washington, D.C., 1960s-1970s
criminal-personality.story: Psychiatrist Samuel Yochelson set out to treat men who had committed serious crimes, many found not guilty by reason of insanity, using standard insight therapy. He concluded it did not work: the men used it to find excuses. Working with psychologist Stanton Samenow, he catalogued recurring thinking patterns, such as seeing oneself as a victim, refusing obligations and assuming others owe you, and focused on changing those patterns directly.
criminal-personality.shows: Habitual ways of thinking can drive repeated harmful behavior; naming them is a foundation for cognitive approaches used in corrections today.
criminal-personality.caveat: Their work had no comparison group, drew on an unusual sample and painted offenders in sweeping terms; later cognitive-behavioral programs became more balanced and evidence-based.

gross-reappraisal.title: Gross's film study: hide it or rethink it
gross-reappraisal.story: Volunteers watched a gruesome medical film. Some were told simply to watch, some to hide their feelings so no one could tell, and some to view it with the detached eye of a medical professional. Those who hid their feelings looked calm, but their bodies were more stirred up and later they remembered less. Those who rethought the scene actually felt less disgust, without the physical cost.
gross-reappraisal.shows: Changing how we interpret a situation, reappraisal, tends to work better than stuffing emotions down, suppression, which only hides the surface.
gross-reappraisal.caveat: Suppression is not always harmful; in some cultures and in some dangerous situations, hiding feelings is wise. Flexibility matters more than one strategy.
gross-reappraisal.source: Gross (1998, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology); Richards & Gross (2000)

affect-labeling.title: Name it to tame it
affect-labeling.story: Volunteers in a brain scanner looked at photos of angry or frightened faces. When they matched the face to another face, the amygdala, an alarm center, responded strongly. When they picked a word naming the emotion, such as 'angry', the amygdala quieted and a region in the front of the brain became more active. A related study found that people afraid of spiders who described their fear aloud while approaching one showed less physical arousal.
affect-labeling.shows: Putting feelings into words, affect labeling, partly calms the emotional alarm, which is why naming a feeling is a first step in managing it.
affect-labeling.caveat: Effects in the lab are modest and labeling does not erase strong emotions; it works best as one tool among several.
affect-labeling.source: Lieberman et al. (2007, Psychological Science); Kircanski et al. (2012)

bushman-catharsis.title: Venting does not drain anger
bushman-catharsis.story: Students were insulted by another participant about an essay they had written. Some then hit a punching bag while thinking about the person who insulted them; others hit it while thinking about fitness; others sat quietly. Afterwards each had a chance to blast the insulter with unpleasant noise. Those who had vented while thinking of the insulter were the angriest and most aggressive. Sitting quietly worked best.
bushman-catharsis.shows: Venting rehearses anger rather than releasing it; calming the body and changing thoughts lowers it.
bushman-catharsis.caveat: Lab aggression measures are artificial, but the finding fits a broad body of research against the 'let off steam' idea.
bushman-catharsis.source: Brad Bushman (2002, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin)

sapolsky-baboons.title: Sapolsky's baboons and the gentle troop
sapolsky-baboons.who_when: Robert Sapolsky, wild baboons in Kenya, 1970s onward
sapolsky-baboons.story: For decades Sapolsky darted wild baboons to measure stress hormones. Low-ranking males, constantly harassed, had chronically high stress hormones and worse health. Then one troop changed: the most aggressive males fed at a tourist lodge garbage dump, caught tuberculosis and died. The surviving troop became calmer and more affectionate, with less stress for low-ranking animals, and the gentler culture persisted for years as new males joined and learned it.
sapolsky-baboons.shows: Chronic social stress, being at the bottom with no control, wears the body down, and the culture of a group can change and be taught to newcomers.
sapolsky-baboons.caveat: Baboons are not humans, and one troop's story is a natural accident rather than an experiment; still it fits human research on status and health.
sapolsky-baboons.source: Robert Sapolsky, A Primate's Memoir (2001); Sapolsky & Share (2004, PLoS Biology)

selye.title: Selye's clumsy discovery of stress
selye.story: Young Selye was hunting for a new hormone by injecting rats with extracts. The rats developed swollen adrenal glands, stomach ulcers and shrunken immune tissue. But the same happened when he injected salt water, or simply exposed rats to cold or hard exercise, and even his own awkward handling seemed to stress them. He concluded the body mounts the same general response to almost any heavy demand, and popularized the word stress.
selye.shows: Very different pressures trigger one shared body alarm; kept switched on for long periods, it damages health.
selye.caveat: Later research showed stress responses are more specific than Selye thought and depend heavily on how a person appraises a situation.
selye.source: Hans Selye, The Stress of Life (1956)

frankl.title: Frankl's search for meaning
frankl.who_when: Viktor Frankl, Austrian psychiatrist, Nazi concentration camps, 1942-1945
frankl.story: Frankl, a Vienna psychiatrist, was deported with his family; his wife, parents and brother died in the camps. In Theresienstadt, Auschwitz and Dachau subcamps he watched how prisoners responded to the same horror. Those who held on to a reason to live, a loved one, unfinished work, even a sense of responsibility to their suffering, seemed more able to endure. He later wrote that people can be stripped of everything except the freedom to choose their attitude.
frankl.shows: Meaning and purpose are powerful protective factors, even under extreme loss of freedom; his logotherapy built on this.
frankl.caveat: His book is a memoir and a philosophy, not a study; survival in the camps depended overwhelmingly on luck and circumstance, which Frankl himself acknowledged.
frankl.source: Viktor Frankl, Man's Search for Meaning (1946)

holmes-rahe.title: Holmes and Rahe's stress points
holmes-rahe.who_when: Thomas Holmes and Richard Rahe, University of Washington, 1967
holmes-rahe.story: Holmes and Rahe asked people to rate how much readjustment various life events demanded, and built a scale. Death of a spouse topped the list, followed by divorce and separation; a jail term ranked high. Surprisingly, happy events were on it too: marriage, a new job, holidays, even Christmas. People who piled up many points in a year tended to report more illness afterwards.
holmes-rahe.shows: Change itself is stressful, good or bad, so reentry, with many changes at once, is a stress overload even when the changes are welcome.
holmes-rahe.caveat: The scale ignores how a person interprets events and how much support they have; links to illness are modest. Treat it as a conversation starter.
holmes-rahe.source: Holmes & Rahe (1967, Journal of Psychosomatic Research)

lazarus-film.title: Lazarus and the soundtrack that changed fear
lazarus-film.who_when: Richard Lazarus and colleagues, University of California, Berkeley, 1960s
lazarus-film.story: Volunteers watched a disturbing film of a painful initiation rite. One group heard a narration stressing the pain; another heard a detached, anthropological commentary; a third heard that the experience was not really so bad. Same images, very different body reactions: the detached and reassuring soundtracks led to far less physical stress than the painful one. The point was not that the scene was harmless, but that the meaning attached to it changed how hard the body reacted.
lazarus-film.shows: Stress depends on how we appraise an event, not just on the event; this is the backbone of cognitive approaches to emotion.
lazarus-film.caveat: Lab films are not real trauma; reappraisal has limits when events are truly dangerous or ongoing.
lazarus-film.source: Speisman, Lazarus et al. (1964); Lazarus & Folkman, Stress, Appraisal, and Coping (1984)

pennebaker-writing.title: Pennebaker's writing cure
pennebaker-writing.story: College students wrote for fifteen minutes on four consecutive days. Some wrote about trivial topics; others wrote about the most upsetting experience of their lives, their deepest thoughts and feelings about it. The emotional writers felt worse right after writing, but in the following months they visited the campus health center less often than the others. Writing that grew more insightful over the days, using words like because and realize, was linked to the greatest benefit.
pennebaker-writing.shows: Turning painful experiences into words, in private, can help people make sense of them and ease their weight, the logic behind unsent letters and journaling.
pennebaker-writing.caveat: Later research found the benefits real but modest and inconsistent; writing is not a substitute for treatment for serious trauma.
pennebaker-writing.source: Pennebaker & Beall (1986, Journal of Abnormal Psychology)

capilano-bridge.title: Love on a shaky bridge
capilano-bridge.who_when: Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron, Capilano Suspension Bridge, Vancouver, 1974
capilano-bridge.story: A woman approached men who had just crossed either a swaying, narrow suspension bridge high above a canyon or a low, sturdy bridge. She asked them to complete a short questionnaire and gave her phone number in case they had questions. More men from the scary bridge called her, and their stories contained more sexual imagery. They may have mistaken pounding hearts for attraction.
capilano-bridge.shows: Physical arousal is easy to mislabel; excitement from danger or drugs can be confused with attraction, which is one way sex and using become entangled.
capilano-bridge.caveat: A small field study; later work suggests misattribution of arousal is real but weaker and more conditional than the famous story implies.

ekman-faces.title: Ekman's faces in Papua New Guinea
ekman-faces.who_when: Paul Ekman and colleagues, Fore people of Papua New Guinea, late 1960s
ekman-faces.story: Ekman traveled to a remote group who had seen little Western media. He told them short stories, such as someone's child has died, and asked them to pick the matching face from photographs of Americans; he also photographed their own expressions. Many matches lined up with Western judgments for emotions such as happiness, sadness, anger and fear. Expressions of fear and surprise were the most often confused with each other.
ekman-faces.shows: Some facial expressions of emotion are widely shared across cultures, so learning to read faces is a real social skill.
ekman-faces.caveat: Lisa Feldman Barrett and others argue faces are far less reliable signals than claimed: context, culture and individual style matter a lot. Check a guess by asking.
ekman-faces.source: Paul Ekman, Emotions Revealed (2003); Lisa Feldman Barrett, How Emotions Are Made (2017)

relaxation-response.title: Benson's relaxation response
relaxation-response.story: Benson, a cardiologist, studied people who practiced Transcendental Meditation and found that while meditating their breathing slowed, oxygen use fell and the body shifted out of stress mode. He argued that no special mantra or belief system was needed: sitting quietly, repeating a word or phrase and gently returning to it when the mind wandered produced the same calming response.
relaxation-response.shows: The body has a built-in off-switch for the stress response that can be trained with simple daily practice.
relaxation-response.caveat: Benefits for blood pressure and anxiety are generally modest; it supports treatment rather than replacing it.

cyberball.title: Cyberball: the pain of being left out
cyberball.who_when: Kipling Williams; Naomi Eisenberger, Matthew Lieberman and Williams, UCLA, 2003
cyberball.story: Williams got the idea after two strangers in a park included him in a frisbee game, then suddenly stopped throwing to him, and he felt surprisingly hurt. He created a computer ball-tossing game in which the other 'players' stop passing to you. Even knowing it was just a computer game, people felt sad and angry, and brain scans showed activity in regions also involved in physical pain distress.
cyberball.shows: Rejection hurts in a real, bodily way, which is why it can trigger anger or relapse and deserves a coping plan.
cyberball.caveat: The overlap between social and physical pain in the brain is debated; the hurt of exclusion, though, is consistently found.

mi-origins.title: How motivational interviewing began
mi-origins.who_when: William R. Miller, Norway and the USA, 1980-1983; later with Stephen Rollnick
mi-origins.story: In one study Miller ran, the drinkers whose counselors showed the most accurate empathy drank much less months later, a finding that surprised him. Later, on sabbatical in Norway, young psychologists asked him to show how he worked with problem drinkers. As they kept asking why he did each thing, he spelled out an approach that avoided arguing and drew out people's own reasons for change. His 1983 article named it motivational interviewing.
mi-origins.shows: Arguing with someone tends to strengthen resistance; listening for and reflecting their own reasons for change builds motivation.
mi-origins.caveat: MI has strong but mixed evidence; effects vary widely by counselor skill, and it works best as a way of being with people rather than a set of tricks.
mi-origins.source: Miller (1983, Behavioural Psychotherapy); Miller & Rollnick, Motivational Interviewing (1991)

stages-of-change.title: The self-changers who mapped the stages
stages-of-change.who_when: James Prochaska and Carlo DiClemente, University of Rhode Island, early 1980s
stages-of-change.story: Instead of asking how therapy changes people, Prochaska and DiClemente studied smokers, including many who quit on their own. They found people moved through recognizable phases: not yet considering change, thinking about it, getting ready, taking action, and keeping it up, often cycling back and trying again. Different strategies seemed to help at different points. Successful quitters often went around the cycle several times before the change stuck.
stages-of-change.shows: Change is a process over time, not a single decision, and relapse is a common part of the cycle rather than proof of failure.
stages-of-change.caveat: Critics such as Robert West argue the stages are arbitrary lines on a continuum and that stage-matched programs have not consistently beaten others. It remains a useful map, not a law.
stages-of-change.source: Prochaska & DiClemente (1983, Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology)

implementation-intentions.title: If-then plans and the Christmas report
implementation-intentions.who_when: Peter Gollwitzer and Veronika Brandstätter, Germany, 1997
implementation-intentions.story: Students heading home for Christmas were asked to write a report on how they spent Christmas Eve within two days. Some also wrote down exactly when and where they would write it. Those who made that specific plan were far more likely to send the report on time. Across many later studies, 'if situation X, then I will do Y' plans helped people follow through.
implementation-intentions.shows: Deciding in advance exactly when, where and how you will act turns intentions into action and gives a ready response for risky moments.
implementation-intentions.caveat: Effects are real on average but vary; plans fail if they are unrealistic or the goal is not truly wanted.

delay-discounting.title: Money now or more money later
delay-discounting.who_when: Gregory Madden, Nancy Petry, Gary Badger and Warren Bickel, University of Vermont, 1997
delay-discounting.story: People dependent on opioids and people without addiction made a series of choices such as a smaller amount of money today versus a larger amount in a month. The opioid-dependent group discounted future rewards much more steeply, accepting much smaller amounts to get money now. Later studies found similar patterns across many substances, and that steep discounting can improve with recovery.
delay-discounting.shows: Addiction narrows the time horizon; tools that make future consequences vivid, like cost-benefit work and future-self exercises, aim right at this.
delay-discounting.caveat: Not all steep discounting is irrational: when life is unpredictable, taking the sure thing now can make sense, as poverty and prison often teach.

hot-cold-gap.title: The hot-cold empathy gap
hot-cold-gap.who_when: George Loewenstein; Michael Sayette and colleagues, smokers study, 2008
hot-cold-gap.story: Smokers were asked how much money they would need to delay smoking. When asked while calm and not craving, they underestimated how much they would want a cigarette later, when they had been made to crave. In a cool state, people cannot really imagine how strong a hot state will feel. The same gap appears with hunger, sexual arousal and anger: in a calm moment we promise ourselves we will stay in control.
hot-cold-gap.shows: Plans made while calm underestimate craving, so emergency plans must be simple, rehearsed and ready for when thinking shrinks.
hot-cold-gap.caveat: Studies use mild, lab-induced craving; real-life craving is messier, which strengthens rather than weakens the warning.
hot-cold-gap.source: Sayette, Loewenstein et al. (2008, Psychological Science)

behavioral-activation.title: Doing before feeling: behavioral activation
behavioral-activation.who_when: Neil Jacobson and colleagues, University of Washington, 1996; Sona Dimidjian and colleagues, 2006
behavioral-activation.story: Jacobson's team took cognitive therapy for depression apart to see which piece mattered. One group got only the behavioral part: scheduling activities that gave a sense of pleasure or accomplishment. They improved about as much as those who got the full package including work on thoughts. A later trial found behavioral activation performed well against medication for more severe depression.
behavioral-activation.shows: Action can lift mood before motivation arrives; filling time with rewarding activity is a treatment, not just a distraction.
behavioral-activation.caveat: Results in later trials are good but not uniformly superior; thinking work still helps many people.
behavioral-activation.source: Jacobson et al. (1996); Dimidjian et al. (2006)

dweck-mindset.title: Praise for effort versus praise for brains
dweck-mindset.who_when: Claudia Mueller and Carol Dweck, Columbia University, 1998
dweck-mindset.story: Children solved puzzles and were praised either for being smart or for working hard. Then they hit a set of very hard puzzles they failed. Children praised for intelligence were more likely to give up, enjoy the task less and even exaggerate their scores; those praised for effort persisted and chose challenging tasks. Dweck called the two outlooks fixed and growth mindsets.
dweck-mindset.shows: Seeing ability as something that grows with effort helps people treat failure as information rather than a verdict.
dweck-mindset.caveat: Large later studies found mindset interventions have small average effects, larger for struggling students; the idea has been oversold in popular form.
dweck-mindset.source: Mueller & Dweck (1998); Sisk et al. (2018 meta-analysis)

marshmallow.title: The marshmallow test
marshmallow.who_when: Walter Mischel and colleagues, Bing Nursery School, Stanford University, late 1960s-1970s
marshmallow.story: Preschoolers sat alone with a treat. They could eat one now or, if they waited until the researcher returned, get two. Some ate it instantly; others covered their eyes, sang, or pretended it was a cloud. Children who distracted themselves or thought about the treat in a cool way waited longer. Follow-ups years later found that the waiters, on average, did somewhat better in school.
marshmallow.shows: Self-control is largely a set of learnable strategies, especially distraction and changing how you think about the temptation, not just raw willpower.
marshmallow.caveat: A 2018 replication with a larger, more diverse sample by Watts, Duncan and Quan found the link with later achievement much smaller, largely explained by family background. Another study found children waited longer when adults had proven reliable: trust shapes waiting.
marshmallow.source: Walter Mischel, The Marshmallow Test (2014); Watts, Duncan & Quan (2018); Kidd, Palmeri & Aslin (2013)

ego-depletion.title: Ego depletion: the radish study that failed to replicate
ego-depletion.who_when: Roy Baumeister and colleagues, 1998; multi-lab replication, 2016
ego-depletion.story: Hungry students sat near freshly baked cookies. Some were allowed to eat them; others had to eat radishes instead. Afterwards, the radish eaters gave up sooner on an impossible puzzle, suggesting self-control is a limited resource like a muscle that tires. Hundreds of studies followed. But a large replication across many labs in 2016 found almost no effect. The idea had already shaped self-help books and training programs.
ego-depletion.shows: Claims about willpower should be held loosely: the evidence that self-control simply runs out like fuel is now weak.
ego-depletion.caveat: Debate continues; beliefs about willpower may matter, since people who think it is limited seem to tire more. Good routines that reduce temptation remain more reliable than willpower alone.
ego-depletion.source: Baumeister et al. (1998); Hagger et al. (2016, Perspectives on Psychological Science)

white-bear.title: Don't think of a white bear
white-bear.who_when: Daniel Wegner and colleagues, Trinity University, 1987
white-bear.story: Volunteers were asked to talk aloud for five minutes while trying not to think of a white bear, ringing a bell whenever it came to mind. They rang often. Later, when they were allowed to think of the bear, it came up even more than for people who had been told to think about it from the start: a rebound.
white-bear.shows: Trying to force a thought away can make it come back stronger, which is why urges are better noticed and ridden out than fought.
white-bear.caveat: The rebound effect is reliable on average but not universal; distraction with a specific alternative works better than plain suppression.
white-bear.source: Wegner et al. (1987, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology)

urge-surfing.title: Urge surfing and mindfulness-based relapse prevention
urge-surfing.who_when: G. Alan Marlatt, Sarah Bowen and colleagues, University of Washington, 2000s-2014
urge-surfing.story: Marlatt taught clients to treat cravings like ocean waves: notice them rise, peak and fall, without acting or fighting. His team built mindfulness-based relapse prevention and tested it in a randomized trial against standard relapse prevention and usual care. A year after treatment, the mindfulness group reported fewer days of drug use and heavy drinking. Participants practiced staying with cravings in session, observing where they felt them in the body and how they changed from moment to moment.
urge-surfing.shows: Cravings are temporary; watching them with curiosity rather than obeying or battling them lowers their grip.
urge-surfing.caveat: One major trial and smaller studies; results are promising but not uniformly superior to standard relapse prevention.

glueck-men.title: The Glueck men: turning points across a lifetime
glueck-men.who_when: Sheldon and Eleanor Glueck, Boston, 1940s; John Laub and Robert Sampson, follow-ups to age 70
glueck-men.story: In the 1940s the Gluecks studied 500 boys from Massachusetts reform schools and 500 non-delinquent boys. Decades later, Laub and Sampson found the dusty case files in a Harvard Law School basement and traced many of the men, interviewing some near age 70. Nearly all the delinquent boys eventually stopped offending, at different ages. Turning points stood out: a good marriage, steady work, military service, a move, which restructured daily routines and gave them something to lose.
glueck-men.shows: People are not locked into a criminal path; ordinary social bonds and new routines in adulthood can redirect a life, even after serious early trouble.
glueck-men.caveat: The men were white Boston boys of a specific era; the turning points that worked for them, like military service, may look different today. Desistance also involves personal choice, which they stress too.
glueck-men.source: Sampson & Laub, Crime in the Making (1993); Laub & Sampson, Shared Beginnings, Divergent Lives (2003)

maruna-redemption.title: Maruna's redemption scripts
maruna-redemption.story: Maruna interviewed people with long criminal histories in Liverpool, some still offending and some who had stopped. Their stories differed sharply. Those who were persisting told a condemnation script: life is against me, I have no real choice. Those who had desisted told a redemption script: deep down I was always a decent person, bad circumstances led me astray, and now I want to give something back, often by helping others avoid their mistakes.
maruna-redemption.shows: The story people tell about who they are shapes whether change lasts; a hopeful, generous self-story supports desistance.
maruna-redemption.caveat: Interviews show association, not cause; desisters may tell better stories because they are doing better. Still, narrative work is now central to desistance research.

good-lives.title: The Good Lives Model
good-lives.who_when: Tony Ward and colleagues, New Zealand and Australia, early 2000s
good-lives.story: Ward, working in sexual offending treatment, argued that programs focused only on managing risk left people with a list of things they must not do and nothing to live for. His Good Lives Model starts from the idea that everyone seeks basic goods, such as relationships, mastery, meaning, autonomy and peace of mind, and that offending is often a harmful way of seeking them. Treatment then helps people build safer ways to get those goods.
good-lives.shows: Reducing risk works better when paired with building a life worth protecting, a strengths-based complement to risk-need-responsivity.
good-lives.caveat: Research on GLM outcomes is still limited; it is best seen as a way to deliver risk-focused treatment more humanely, and debate with risk-need-responsivity researchers continues.

scared-straight.title: Scared Straight backfired
scared-straight.who_when: Rahway State Prison, New Jersey, 1978 documentary; later evaluations by Anthony Petrosino and colleagues
scared-straight.story: Inmates serving life sentences yelled at and threatened visiting teenagers to frighten them away from crime. A television documentary made the program famous and it spread widely. When researchers pooled controlled studies, the teenagers who went through such programs offended somewhat more afterwards than similar teenagers who did not. Many states and countries copied it, and a television series revived the format decades later.
scared-straight.shows: Fear and confrontation are poor teachers of change; programs that build skills and relationships beat scare tactics.
scared-straight.caveat: Studies were mostly older and of varied quality, but they point consistently in the same direction.
scared-straight.source: Petrosino et al., Campbell Collaboration review

cambridge-somerville.title: Cambridge-Somerville: when help harmed
cambridge-somerville.who_when: Richard Cabot, Massachusetts, 1930s-1940s; follow-up by Joan McCord, 1970s
cambridge-somerville.story: Hundreds of boys considered at risk of delinquency were randomly assigned either to receive mentoring, tutoring, medical care and summer camps, or to receive nothing extra. Participants and counselors believed it helped. But when Joan McCord tracked the men some thirty years later, those who got the program had worse outcomes on several measures, such as more serious crime and alcoholism, especially boys sent to summer camp repeatedly with other troubled boys.
cambridge-somerville.shows: Well-meant programs can harm, and grouping high-risk people together can spread risky behavior, so programs need testing and careful design.
cambridge-somerville.caveat: The exact reasons are debated; deviant peer contagion is the leading explanation but not proven.

pager-record.title: The mark of a criminal record
pager-record.story: Pager sent pairs of young men with matched résumés to apply for entry-level jobs; the only planned difference was that one said he had a drug conviction and recent prison time. Applicants with a record got far fewer callbacks. Black applicants were hit harder: those with no record received callbacks at about the rate of white applicants who had one.
pager-record.shows: Employment barriers after prison are real and measurable, so job searches need strategy, persistence and supportive employers, not only motivation.
pager-record.caveat: One city at one time, with a small number of testers; later studies in other cities found similar patterns, and some policies such as ban-the-box have complex effects.
pager-record.source: Devah Pager (2003, American Journal of Sociology); Marked (2007)

prison-education.title: Education behind bars
prison-education.who_when: Lois Davis and colleagues, RAND Corporation, 2013
prison-education.story: RAND pooled decades of studies of education programs in prisons, from basic literacy to college courses and vocational training. People who took part were notably less likely to return to prison than similar people who did not, and somewhat more likely to find work after release. They estimated that the programs more than paid for themselves in reduced incarceration costs.
prison-education.shows: Learning in prison is one of the more reliable investments in reentry, supporting education and job goals.
prison-education.caveat: Most studies were not randomized, so motivated people may have chosen to enroll; RAND tried to weight the stronger studies.
prison-education.source: Davis et al., Evaluating the Effectiveness of Correctional Education (RAND, 2013)

vipassana-prison.title: Meditation in prison
vipassana-prison.who_when: Tihar Jail, Delhi, early 1990s; Donaldson Correctional Facility, Alabama, 2000s; Sarah Bowen and colleagues, Seattle jail study, 2006
vipassana-prison.story: Under prison reformer Kiran Bedi, a ten-day silent Vipassana meditation course was held for many inmates of Tihar, one of India's largest prisons. Similar courses later ran in a maximum-security prison in Alabama, documented in the film The Dhamma Brothers. A study at a Seattle-area jail found that people who completed the course reported less alcohol and drug use after release than those who did not.
vipassana-prison.shows: Mindfulness practice can be learned in the hardest settings and may reduce substance use and reactivity.
vipassana-prison.caveat: People chose to take the course, so motivated participants may differ from others; outcomes after release were self-reported.
vipassana-prison.source: Bowen et al. (2006, Psychology of Addictive Behaviors)

harlow-monkeys.title: Harlow's cloth mother
harlow-monkeys.story: Infant rhesus monkeys were raised with two artificial mothers: one made of bare wire that held a milk bottle, one covered in soft cloth that gave no food. The babies fed briefly from the wire mother but spent most of their time clinging to the cloth one, and ran to it when frightened. Monkeys raised in total isolation became severely disturbed, unable to play, mate or parent.
harlow-monkeys.shows: Comfort and touch, not just food, are basic needs; early deprivation of warmth can have lasting effects on relationships.
harlow-monkeys.caveat: The isolation experiments were cruel and helped spark the animal-rights movement; many scientists today regard them as ethically indefensible.

bowlby-thieves.title: Bowlby's forty-four juvenile thieves
bowlby-thieves.who_when: John Bowlby, London Child Guidance Clinic, published 1944
bowlby-thieves.story: Young psychiatrist John Bowlby studied 44 children referred for stealing and compared them with children referred for other problems. A striking number of the thieves had experienced long separations from their mothers in early childhood, and some seemed emotionally cut off, which he called affectionless. This work grew into attachment theory, the idea that a secure early bond shapes how we handle relationships and stress.
bowlby-thieves.shows: Early disrupted bonds can shape later behavior, including stealing and difficulty trusting, which helps explain without excusing.
bowlby-thieves.caveat: Bowlby's sample was small and his data retrospective; he was later criticized for overstating maternal deprivation and overlooking fathers and other caregivers. Later research shows people can form secure bonds later in life.
bowlby-thieves.source: John Bowlby (1944, International Journal of Psychoanalysis)

strange-situation.title: Ainsworth's Strange Situation
strange-situation.who_when: Mary Ainsworth, Uganda in the 1950s; Baltimore, 1960s-1970s
strange-situation.story: Ainsworth watched one-year-olds in a playroom as their mother left briefly and a stranger came in, then the mother returned. Most babies used the mother as a safe base, protested when she left and were quickly comforted on her return. Others ignored her return or clung angrily and could not be soothed. These patterns tracked how sensitively mothers had responded to their babies at home.
strange-situation.shows: Sensitive, reliable caregiving teaches a child that people can be trusted; children of unpredictable parents learn to cope in other ways.
strange-situation.caveat: The test was developed in Western middle-class families; patterns vary by culture, and a child's attachment style can change.
strange-situation.source: Ainsworth et al., Patterns of Attachment (1978)

romanian-orphans.title: Romanian orphans and the Bucharest project
romanian-orphans.who_when: Charles Nelson, Nathan Fox and Charles Zeanah, Bucharest Early Intervention Project, from 2000
romanian-orphans.story: Under Romania's former regime, many children grew up in grim institutions with little individual care. In this project, young children in institutions were randomly assigned either to stay or to be placed with trained foster families. Children placed in foster care did better in thinking, emotional bonds and mental health, and those placed earlier, generally before about age two, gained the most.
romanian-orphans.shows: Responsive caregiving is a biological need for children, and it is never too late to help, though earlier is better.
romanian-orphans.caveat: Randomizing children raised ethical concerns, addressed partly because foster care did not yet exist there; some effects shrank in later follow-ups.
romanian-orphans.source: Nelson, Fox & Zeanah, Romania's Abandoned Children (2014)

still-face.title: The still face experiment
still-face.story: A mother plays face to face with her baby, smiling and cooing, and the baby responds. Then, on cue, she turns briefly away and turns back with a blank, unresponsive face. Within moments the baby tries everything: smiling, pointing, reaching, then becomes distressed and turns away. When the mother re-engages, the baby recovers. Video of these brief episodes is still used in training today because the baby's reaction is so immediate.
still-face.shows: Even infants need emotional responsiveness; being ignored is stressful, and repair after a disconnection matters more than perfection.
still-face.caveat: Short lab episodes do not cause harm on their own; the concern is chronic unresponsiveness, for example during a parent's depression or substance use.

gottman-lab.title: Gottman's Love Lab
gottman-lab.who_when: John Gottman and colleagues, University of Washington, 1980s onward
gottman-lab.story: Gottman observed couples discussing a disagreement in his lab, recording words, faces and heart rates, and followed them for years. Couples who later split tended to show four patterns he called the four horsemen: criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling, with contempt the strongest warning sign. Stable couples also responded to each other's small bids for attention, a comment or a sigh, rather than ignoring them.
gottman-lab.shows: How partners handle conflict and small moments of connection predicts whether relationships last, and these are learnable skills.
gottman-lab.caveat: Famous claims that he can predict divorce with near-perfect accuracy have been criticized as overstating what the statistics show.
gottman-lab.source: John Gottman, The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work (1999)

hand-holding.title: Holding a hand under threat
hand-holding.who_when: James Coan, Hillary Schaefer and Richard Davidson, University of Wisconsin, 2006
hand-holding.story: Married women lay in a brain scanner, told they might receive a mild electric shock. Sometimes they held their husband's hand, sometimes a stranger's, sometimes no one's. Holding the husband's hand calmed threat-related brain activity most, especially for women in happier marriages; even a stranger's hand helped a little. The researcher called the idea social baseline theory: the brain expects to face threats with others and works harder when alone.
hand-holding.shows: Social support works through the body: having a trusted person near literally reduces the brain's threat response.
hand-holding.caveat: A small sample of married women; the effect depends on relationship quality, not just presence.

capitalization.title: Responding to good news
capitalization.story: Gable studied what happens when people share good news, like a promotion, with a partner. She found four response styles, from enthusiastic and curious, to lukewarm, to deflating, to ignoring. Couples whose partners usually responded with genuine, active interest reported more trust and satisfaction, sometimes more than from how they handled bad news. Responding in a flat, distracted or deflating way, by contrast, seemed to chip away at closeness even when it was not meant badly.
capitalization.shows: Celebrating someone else's wins, and having your own celebrated, strengthens relationships, so marking positive events is a social skill.
capitalization.caveat: Mostly self-report and couples research; the pattern is consistent but its size varies.
capitalization.source: Gable et al. (2004, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology)

rogers-gloria.title: Carl Rogers on film
rogers-gloria.who_when: Carl Rogers, recorded sessions from the 1940s; the 'Gloria' films, 1965
rogers-gloria.story: At a time when therapy happened behind closed doors, Rogers recorded and published real sessions so others could study them.
