In a famous 1965 film, a client called Gloria spoke with three therapists in turn: Rogers, Fritz Perls and Albert Ellis. Rogers mostly listened, reflected her feelings and accepted her without judgment; viewers have argued about the three styles ever since.
rogers-gloria.shows: Accurate listening, warmth and genuineness are powerful in their own right; research on the therapeutic relationship has built on this.
rogers-gloria.caveat: One filmed session cannot show what works best; Gloria herself later described her impressions, which do not settle the debate.
rogers-gloria.source: Carl Rogers, On Becoming a Person (1961)

claudia-black.title: Don't talk, don't trust, don't feel
claudia-black.who_when: Claudia Black, clinical work with children of alcoholics, 1970s-1981
claudia-black.story: Working with children growing up with alcoholic parents, Black noticed the same unwritten family rules again and again: don't talk about the drinking, don't trust anyone with what is happening, and don't feel or show emotions. Others, such as Sharon Wegscheider-Cruse, described roles children take on to survive, like the hero, the scapegoat, the lost child and the mascot. Many of these children grew into adults who struggled to trust, ask for help or know what they felt.
claudia-black.shows: Families adapt to addiction with silent rules and roles that protect in the short run but cost the children later; naming them opens a way out.
claudia-black.caveat: These ideas come from clinical observation, not controlled research; studies find children of alcoholics vary widely, and fixed roles are best seen as a metaphor.
claudia-black.source: Claudia Black, It Will Never Happen to Me (1981)

craft.title: CRAFT: helping families help without confrontation
craft.who_when: Robert Meyers, William Miller and Scott Tonigan, University of New Mexico, 1999
craft.story: Families of people refusing treatment were randomly assigned to one of three approaches: Al-Anon-style support, the confrontational Johnson Institute intervention where family members surprise the person, or CRAFT, which teaches families to reward sober behavior, stop shielding the person from consequences and pick good moments to suggest help. CRAFT families got their loved ones into treatment far more often; many families in the confrontational group never went through with it.
craft.shows: Loved ones can influence change through warmth, rewards and timing more effectively than through confrontation, and they can improve their own wellbeing too.
craft.caveat: Results depend on trained counselors; Al-Anon still benefited family members' own wellbeing, its main goal.
craft.source: Miller, Meyers & Tonigan (1999, Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology)

kauai-resilience.title: The children of Kauai
kauai-resilience.who_when: Emmy Werner and Ruth Smith, island of Kauai, Hawaii, from 1955
kauai-resilience.story: Werner followed every child born on Kauai in 1955 for decades. About a third grew up with serious risks such as poverty, parental alcoholism or mental illness, and family conflict. Many of them developed problems, yet a sizable share grew into caring, competent adults. Common threads included at least one steady adult who cared about them, sometimes a grandparent or teacher, and later turning points like education or military service.
kauai-resilience.shows: Resilience is common and is built through relationships; one reliable adult can change a child's trajectory.
kauai-resilience.caveat: One island community; protective factors are associations, and resilience is not a fixed trait some children simply have.
kauai-resilience.source: Werner & Smith, Vulnerable but Invincible (1982); Overcoming the Odds (1992)

baumrind-styles.title: Baumrind's parenting styles
baumrind-styles.who_when: Diana Baumrind, University of California, Berkeley, 1960s
baumrind-styles.story: Baumrind observed preschool children and their parents at home and in the lab. She described three main styles: authoritarian parents demanded obedience with little warmth; permissive parents were warm but set few limits; authoritative parents combined warmth with clear, explained rules. Children of authoritative parents tended to be the most self-reliant and cooperative. Later researchers added a fourth, neglectful style.
baumrind-styles.shows: Warmth and structure together work better than either alone, a useful frame for reflecting on how we were raised and how we parent.
baumrind-styles.caveat: The fit of each style varies across cultures and circumstances; in dangerous neighborhoods firmer parenting can be protective. Correlations do not prove the style caused the outcomes.

ace-study.title: The ACE study: the dropouts who explained everything
ace-study.who_when: Vincent Felitti, Kaiser Permanente, San Diego; Robert Anda, CDC; published 1998
ace-study.story: Felitti ran a weight-loss clinic and was puzzled when some of his most successful patients dropped out just as they were losing weight. Interviews revealed many had suffered childhood sexual abuse; for some, weight felt like protection. With the CDC he surveyed thousands of patients about childhood adversities such as abuse, neglect and a household member with addiction or in prison. The more adversities people reported, the higher their adult risk of addiction, depression, heart disease and early death.
ace-study.shows: Childhood adversity is common and powerfully linked to later health and substance use; often the 'problem' began as a solution to pain.
ace-study.caveat: Reports were retrospective and the original sample was mostly insured, middle-class adults. An ACE score shows group risk, not an individual's fate, and should not be used to label people.
ace-study.source: Felitti, Anda et al. (1998, American Journal of Preventive Medicine)

kubler-ross.title: Kübler-Ross and the five stages
kubler-ross.who_when: Elisabeth Kübler-Ross, University of Chicago hospitals, 1960s
kubler-ross.story: At a time when doctors often avoided talking to dying patients, psychiatrist Kübler-Ross interviewed hundreds of them in front of medical students, asking what they were going through. Her 1969 book described denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance. The stages entered popular culture as a map for every kind of loss. She later applied the stages to grief more broadly in a book written with David Kessler.
kubler-ross.shows: Giving dying and grieving people space to talk was revolutionary, and the stages name feelings many people recognize.
kubler-ross.caveat: The stages came from people facing their own death, not from bereaved families, and research does not support them as a fixed sequence. Kübler-Ross herself said people move among them in any order.
kubler-ross.source: Elisabeth Kübler-Ross, On Death and Dying (1969)

bonanno-resilience.title: Grief is more resilient than we think
bonanno-resilience.story: Bonanno followed people who lost spouses, some since before the death. The most common pattern was not long, deep depression but resilience: real sadness that came in waves, alongside moments of laughter and normal functioning, with steady recovery. A smaller group had chronic grief, and some who were depressed before the loss actually improved afterwards. He argues that the culture of 'grief work', insisting everyone must deeply process a loss, can pressure resilient people unnecessarily.
bonanno-resilience.shows: Grief takes many shapes; feeling okay at times is not denial, and people who stay stuck may need extra help.
bonanno-resilience.caveat: Most data come from Western spousal loss; sudden, violent or stigmatized losses, such as overdose deaths, can be harder.
bonanno-resilience.source: George Bonanno, The Other Side of Sadness (2009)

worthington-forgiveness.title: A forgiveness researcher tested by murder
worthington-forgiveness.story: Worthington had spent years studying forgiveness when his elderly mother was murdered in her home during a burglary in 1996. He described his rage and the urge for revenge, then using his own model, which included recalling the hurt, empathizing with the offender, and choosing to forgive, to work through it. He has written that forgiving did not mean excusing the crime or giving up on justice.
worthington-forgiveness.shows: Forgiveness is an inner process of releasing bitterness, separate from reconciliation or excusing harm, and it can benefit the forgiver.
worthington-forgiveness.caveat: A personal account by a researcher; forgiveness interventions show modest benefits in studies, and no one should be pressured to forgive.

restorative-justice.title: Victims meeting offenders
restorative-justice.who_when: Lawrence Sherman and Heather Strang, randomized trials in Australia and the UK, 1990s-2000s
restorative-justice.story: Victims and offenders who agreed were randomly assigned either to a facilitated face-to-face conference or to normal court processing. In conferences, offenders heard directly how the crime affected the victim and their family, and together they discussed repair. Victims who took part generally reported less fear and anger and more sense of justice; some trials found fewer repeat offenses. Facilitators prepared both sides carefully beforehand.
restorative-justice.shows: Hearing victims' experiences directly can build empathy and accountability in ways punishment alone rarely does.
restorative-justice.caveat: Effects on reoffending were mixed across trials and offense types, and taking part must be voluntary and safe for victims.
restorative-justice.source: Strang & Sherman, Restorative Justice: The Evidence (2007)

brainstorming.title: Brainstorming: alone first
brainstorming.who_when: Alex Osborn, 1950s; Donald Taylor and colleagues, Yale, 1958; Michael Diehl and Wolfgang Stroebe, 1987
brainstorming.story: Advertising executive Alex Osborn popularized group brainstorming: say every idea, no criticism allowed. Researchers then compared real groups with the same number of people working separately whose ideas were pooled afterwards. Again and again, the separate individuals produced more and often better ideas. In groups, people wait their turn and forget ideas, worry about judgment, and coast on others. Even so, people in groups usually believed they had been more creative.
brainstorming.shows: Quantity of options and suspended judgment help problem solving, but people should first jot ideas alone, then share and combine them.
brainstorming.caveat: Groups still help with evaluating and building on ideas, and well-run group methods can reduce the losses.
brainstorming.source: Diehl & Stroebe (1987, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology)

feedback-backfire.title: When feedback makes things worse
feedback-backfire.who_when: Avraham Kluger and Angelo DeNisi, review published 1996
feedback-backfire.story: Kluger and DeNisi pooled hundreds of studies on giving people feedback about their performance. On average feedback helped, but in a sizable share of studies it actually made performance worse. Feedback aimed at the task, what to do differently, tended to help; feedback that drew attention to the person and their self-image tended to hurt. Praise and criticism focused on someone's general worth fared worst.
feedback-backfire.shows: Criticism lands best when it is about behavior and next steps, and people take it in better when they can separate the message from their worth.
feedback-backfire.caveat: Wide variety of settings and measures; the pattern is robust but individual cases depend on relationship and tone.

peer-chicken.title: Teens, peers and the driving game
peer-chicken.who_when: Margo Gardner and Laurence Steinberg, Temple University, 2005
peer-chicken.story: Adolescents, young adults and older adults played a computer driving game where they could stop at yellow lights or risk running them. Alone, all groups took similar risks. With two friends watching, teenagers took far more risks, young adults somewhat more, and older adults about the same. Later brain scans showed the reward system lighting up more for teens when peers were present.
peer-chicken.shows: Being watched by peers amplifies risk taking, especially in younger people, so plans to say no need to include who will be there.
peer-chicken.caveat: Lab driving is not real driving; the effect weakens with age but does not vanish.
peer-chicken.source: Gardner & Steinberg (2005, Developmental Psychology); Chein et al. (2011)

beck-thoughts.title: Beck notices the hidden stream of thought
beck-thoughts.who_when: Aaron Beck, University of Pennsylvania, early 1960s
beck-thoughts.story: Beck, trained as a psychoanalyst, was studying depressed patients, expecting to find hidden anger. Instead, during sessions, he noticed patients had quick, unspoken thoughts running alongside what they said, such as 'he's bored with me' or 'I'm failing at this too'. These automatic thoughts were negative, rapid and believed without question. Teaching patients to catch and test them became cognitive therapy.
beck-thoughts.shows: Fast, automatic thoughts shape feelings and behavior; catching and checking them is a core skill in CBT.
beck-thoughts.caveat: Beck's own account, retold often; the therapy he built has strong evidence, though the idea that thoughts always come first in emotion is debated.
beck-thoughts.source: Aaron Beck, Cognitive Therapy and the Emotional Disorders (1976)

ellis-garden.title: Albert Ellis and the hundred conversations
ellis-garden.who_when: Albert Ellis, Bronx Botanical Garden, New York, early 1930s (his own account)
ellis-garden.story: As a shy nineteen-year-old, Ellis gave himself an assignment: during one summer month, sit next to every woman alone on a bench in the botanical garden and start a conversation within a minute. He later said he spoke with about a hundred women. Almost all conversations went nowhere and only one agreed to a date, and she did not show up. But he lost his fear, because the catastrophe he had imagined never happened.
ellis-garden.shows: Testing beliefs through action shows that rejection is unpleasant but survivable; Ellis built REBT on disputing such catastrophic beliefs.
ellis-garden.caveat: The story is Ellis's own and was polished over decades; REBT has evidence, but this tale is an anecdote.

mbsr.title: Kabat-Zinn's stress clinic
mbsr.who_when: Jon Kabat-Zinn, University of Massachusetts Medical Center, 1979
mbsr.story: Kabat-Zinn, a molecular biologist who practiced meditation, persuaded the hospital to let him teach an eight-week course to patients with chronic pain and other conditions that medicine could not fix. Patients learned to pay attention to breath, body sensations and thoughts without judging them. Many reported less suffering from pain even when the pain itself remained, and the program, Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction, spread worldwide.
mbsr.shows: Changing the relationship to pain and thoughts can reduce suffering when the sensation itself cannot be removed.
mbsr.caveat: Early studies were uncontrolled; later trials show modest-to-moderate benefits, and mindfulness is not helpful for everyone.

minnesota-starvation.title: The Minnesota starvation experiment
minnesota-starvation.who_when: Ancel Keys and colleagues, University of Minnesota, 1944-1945
minnesota-starvation.story: Thirty-six conscientious objectors volunteered to live on half rations for months so researchers could learn how to refeed starving people after the war. As they lost weight, the men became obsessed with food, collecting recipes and dragging meals out for hours. Many grew irritable, depressed and withdrawn, and some struggled to control eating long after the experiment ended. Some had binge eating episodes after the experiment ended.
minnesota-starvation.shows: Hunger changes mood, thinking and impulse control; skipped meals and poor nutrition in early recovery are relapse risks, not trivia.
minnesota-starvation.caveat: It would be unethical today; the men were volunteers and many later said they were glad to have helped.
minnesota-starvation.source: Keys et al., The Biology of Human Starvation (1950)

bus-conductors.title: London bus conductors and heart attacks
bus-conductors.story: Morris compared drivers and conductors on London's double-decker buses. Both groups came from similar backgrounds, but drivers sat all day while conductors climbed up and down the stairs collecting fares. Conductors had noticeably fewer heart attacks, and theirs were less often fatal. It was one of the first studies to link daily physical activity with heart health. He went on to show similar findings among postal workers who walked their routes compared with office clerks.
bus-conductors.shows: Ordinary movement, built into daily life, protects the heart; exercise does not need a gym.
bus-conductors.caveat: Later work found drivers tended to be heavier even when hired, so not all the difference was due to activity; later studies confirmed the core link.

randy-gardner.title: Randy Gardner's eleven days awake
randy-gardner.who_when: Randy Gardner, San Diego, December 1963-January 1964; observed by sleep researcher William Dement
randy-gardner.story: For a school science project, seventeen-year-old Gardner stayed awake for about eleven days. As the days passed he became moody, had trouble concentrating and remembering, slurred his speech and at times mistook objects for people. After the attempt he slept about fourteen hours and recovered quickly. Dement, who stayed with him in the final days, reported that he could still beat him at pinball near the end, yet struggled with simple tasks like counting backwards.
randy-gardner.shows: Sleep loss rapidly degrades mood, memory and judgment, the same functions needed to resist cravings.
randy-gardner.caveat: His fast recovery does not mean sleep loss is harmless; chronic short sleep is linked to many health problems, and record attempts are now discouraged as dangerous.

tuskegee.title: The Tuskegee syphilis study
tuskegee.who_when: US Public Health Service, Macon County, Alabama, 1932-1972
tuskegee.story: Government doctors enrolled hundreds of poor Black men, most with syphilis, telling them they were being treated for 'bad blood'. Even after penicillin became the standard cure in the 1940s, the men were kept from treatment so researchers could study the disease's course. Wives and children were infected. The study ended only after whistle-blower Peter Buxtun took the story to the press in 1972.
tuskegee.shows: Medical mistrust in many communities has real roots; respectful, honest care and consent are the foundation of health work.
tuskegee.caveat: Sometimes misreported as doctors infecting the men; they did not infect them, but they deliberately withheld treatment, which was devastating.

patient-zero-myth.title: The myth of 'Patient Zero'
patient-zero-myth.who_when: Gaëtan Dugas; genetic study by Michael Worobey and colleagues, 2016
patient-zero-myth.story: Early AIDS researchers studying a cluster of cases labeled one man as 'Patient O', for Outside California. The letter was misread as zero, and a bestselling book and the press turned Dugas, a flight attendant, into the man who brought AIDS to America. In 2016, genetic analysis of old blood samples showed HIV had been circulating in the United States for years before him.
patient-zero-myth.shows: Blame stories spread fast and stigma attaches to individuals, while infections actually spread through networks long before anyone notices.
patient-zero-myth.caveat: Dugas did have many partners and was one of many early cases; the myth was in calling him the origin.

kinsey.title: Kinsey's surveys and the prisoners in the sample
kinsey.who_when: Alfred Kinsey and colleagues, Indiana University, 1948 and 1953
kinsey.story: Kinsey, a biologist who had studied gall wasps, interviewed thousands of Americans in detail about their sexual lives. His reports showed that many behaviors considered rare or deviant were common, shocking the public and opening frank discussion of sexuality. His team asked hundreds of questions in face-to-face interviews, coded so that answers stayed confidential, and trained interviewers to ask frankly without showing judgment so people would answer honestly.
kinsey.shows: What people do sexually varies widely, and shame often rests on mistaken ideas about what is normal.
kinsey.caveat: His samples were not random; volunteers and some groups, including men in prison, were overrepresented, so his percentages are not reliable. His methods also raised ethical questions.
kinsey.source: Kinsey et al., Sexual Behavior in the Human Male (1948)

lorig-self-management.title: Patients teaching patients
lorig-self-management.who_when: Kate Lorig and colleagues, Stanford University, 1990s
lorig-self-management.story: Lorig developed a six-week workshop for people with chronic conditions such as arthritis, heart disease and lung disease, led by trained volunteers who themselves lived with a chronic illness. Participants practiced action plans, problem solving and talking with doctors. Studies found they felt more confident managing their health and some used hospitals less. Peers living with the same struggles were the teachers.
lorig-self-management.shows: Confidence in managing your own condition, self-efficacy, is a key ingredient in living with chronic illness alongside addiction recovery.
lorig-self-management.caveat: Effects on health measures are modest and vary; it complements medical care rather than replacing it.

scarcity-farmers.title: Scarcity and the sugarcane farmers
scarcity-farmers.who_when: Anandi Mani, Sendhil Mullainathan, Eldar Shafir and Jiaying Zhao, Tamil Nadu, India, 2013
scarcity-farmers.story: Sugarcane farmers in India receive most of their income once a year at harvest. Researchers tested the same farmers before harvest, when money was tight, and after, when they had been paid. Before harvest, they scored worse on tests of reasoning and attention. Lab studies with shoppers in the United States showed that just thinking about a tough money problem lowered poorer people's scores.
scarcity-farmers.shows: Money worries tax the mind, crowding out planning and self-control; financial stress in reentry is a cognitive load, not a character flaw.
scarcity-farmers.caveat: Some later replications found smaller effects; the general link between scarcity and narrowed attention is still widely accepted.
scarcity-farmers.source: Mani et al. (2013, Science); Mullainathan & Shafir, Scarcity (2013)

william-james.title: William James and the twice-born
william-james.who_when: William James, Gifford Lectures in Edinburgh, 1901-1902
william-james.story: James, a Harvard psychologist and philosopher, gathered first-person accounts of religious experience, from mystics to ordinary people. He was struck by stories of the 'twice-born', people who had hit despair, including drunkards, and then experienced a sudden or gradual sense of being remade. He treated these experiences seriously as psychology, judging them by their fruits in a person's life. He famously remarked that the sway of alcohol over people stems from its power to stimulate mystical feelings that sober life crushes.
william-james.shows: Profound personal change sometimes comes through spiritual experiences, and these can be studied respectfully without settling questions of faith.
william-james.caveat: The accounts were selected and personal; James himself said they could not prove the truth of any religion.
william-james.source: William James, The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902)

langer-plants.title: The nursing home plants
langer-plants.who_when: Ellen Langer and Judith Rodin, a Connecticut nursing home, 1976
langer-plants.story: Residents on one floor were told they were responsible for themselves, could make choices about their days, and were given a plant to care for. Residents on another floor heard that staff would take care of everything, including their plant. Those given responsibility became more active and alert, and at follow-up fewer had died. The difference was small on paper, a few words and a plant, which makes the result striking.
langer-plants.shows: A sense of control and purpose matters at every age, especially later in life when roles and choices shrink.
langer-plants.caveat: A small study whose dramatic mortality finding should be read cautiously; related studies support the importance of control.

harvard-adult-development.title: The Harvard study of adult development
harvard-adult-development.who_when: Grant Study of Harvard men from 1938 and the Glueck inner-city Boston comparison group; directors George Vaillant and later Robert Waldinger
harvard-adult-development.story: Two groups of men have been followed since the late 1930s and early 1940s: Harvard sophomores and boys from poor Boston neighborhoods, the latter originally the non-delinquent comparison group in the Gluecks' study. Decades of records showed that the quality of close relationships in midlife predicted health and happiness in old age better than wealth or cholesterol. George Vaillant also traced the course of alcohol problems, finding alcohol abuse a major destroyer of health and marriages.
harvard-adult-development.shows: Relationships are central to a long, healthy life, and alcohol problems ripple across every area of it.
harvard-adult-development.caveat: The original groups were all men, mostly white Americans; later work added wives and children.
harvard-adult-development.source: George Vaillant, The Natural History of Alcoholism (1983), Triumphs of Experience (2012)

maslow-pyramid.title: Maslow's pyramid that Maslow never drew
maslow-pyramid.who_when: Abraham Maslow, 1943 paper; later research by Louis Tay and Ed Diener, 2011
maslow-pyramid.story: Maslow proposed that people are moved by needs that build on one another: survival, safety, love and belonging, esteem, and becoming the person they can be. Business writers later drew this as a pyramid. A large survey across many countries found that meeting each kind of need was linked to wellbeing, but people could find love or purpose even when basic needs were not fully met.
maslow-pyramid.shows: Unmet needs drive behavior, and drugs often stand in for real needs like belonging and respect.
maslow-pyramid.caveat: The strict ladder is not supported; needs operate together and vary by culture, and Maslow himself did not present a rigid pyramid.
